newsitem.title: USA: US economy shows no signs of overheating - Rivlin.
newsitem.headline: US economy shows no signs of overheating - Rivlin.

text.p: Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alice Rivlin said on Wednesday that the U.S. economy appeared to be growing at its potential without any worrisome signs of overheating.

"The economy seems to be growing about at its trend or potential rate with capacity pretty fully utilized but no clear signs of overheating or serious imbalances," Rivlin said at a dinner ahead of the Senior Executives' Conference of the Mortgage Bankers Association of America.
Rivlin said the U.S. economy was "certainly doing well," and showing the "mixed signals" that suggest trend-like growth.
"One of the remarkable things about the economy at the beginning of 1997 is really how uniform the good news is," said Rivlin.

"The tight labor markets across the country are pretty general ... but I think we should remind ourselves that tight labor markets are basically a good thing not just for the people who have jobs but for the future health of the economy generally," she added.
She noted that wages, particularly low-end wages, have begun to creep up, but said it was a mystery why wages have not risen any more than they have given the current low level of unemployment.
"Even more mystifying to economists ... is why prices have not been rising more rapidly," Rivlin said, noting that productivity gains and global competition could be part of the answer.

Rivlin, who served in the Clinton Administration as deputy budget director and as head of the Office of Management and Budget, also touched upon prospects for a budget deal between Congress and the White House.

"Actually I'm quite optimistic that a budget deal will in fact be cut. After things settle down around the (House) Speaker (Newt Gingrich) and we get through the inauguration I think there will be a serious conversation," she said.
